seo.title: Frequently Asked Questions
seo.description: Clear answers to common questions about Texas divorce, custody, child support, CPS defense, and personal injury claims from Hirani Law Firm.

hero.title: Frequently Asked Questions
hero.description: When you're facing a serious legal issue, the uncertainty can be overwhelming. We have created this page to provide clear, straightforward answers to the most common questions we receive from clients in Houston and the surrounding areas.

items.q: What is the difference between a contested and an uncontested divorce?
items.a: An uncontested divorce is one where both spouses agree on all major issues — property division, custody, support, and debts. A contested divorce is one where the spouses cannot agree on one or more of these issues, requiring negotiation, mediation, or a court to decide. Uncontested cases are generally faster and less expensive.

items.q: How is property divided in a Texas divorce? Is it always 50/50?
items.a: Texas is a community property state, meaning most property acquired during the marriage is subject to division. However, the standard is a "just and right" division, not automatically 50/50. Courts consider factors like earning capacity, fault, and who has custody of the children when dividing the community estate.

items.q: What is spousal support (alimony), and who is eligible for it in Texas?
items.a: Texas allows for "spousal maintenance," but eligibility is limited. It may be awarded when a spouse lacks sufficient property to meet minimum reasonable needs and the marriage lasted 10+ years, or where there is family violence or a disability. Amounts and durations are capped by statute.

items.q: How long does a divorce take in Texas?
items.a: Texas requires a minimum 60-day waiting period from the date of filing before a divorce can be finalized. An uncontested divorce may resolve shortly after that window, while a contested case involving custody or complex property can take several months to over a year.

items.q: Do I need a lawyer for an amicable or uncontested divorce?
items.a: Even when spouses agree, a lawyer ensures the final decree is drafted correctly and fully protects your rights — especially regarding property, retirement accounts, and custody. A small error in an agreed decree can create serious problems years later.

items.q: What is the difference between "custody" and "conservatorship" in Texas?
items.a: Texas law uses the term "conservatorship" rather than "custody." Conservatorship refers to a parent's legal rights and duties regarding the child, while "possession and access" refers to the physical schedule of when each parent has the child.

items.q: How do Texas courts decide who gets custody? What is the "best interest of the child"?
items.a: The court's guiding standard is always the best interest of the child. Judges weigh factors including each parent's ability to care for the child, stability, the child's wishes (if old enough), and any history of family violence or neglect.

items.q: Do Texas courts favor mothers over fathers?
items.a: No. Texas law prohibits courts from favoring a parent based on gender. Both parents start on equal footing, and decisions are based on the best interest of the child. We regularly advocate for father's rights to remain active in their children's lives.

items.q: What is a Standard Possession Order (SPO)?
items.a: A Standard Possession Order is the schedule the Texas Family Code presumes is in a child's best interest for parents who live within 100 miles of each other. It typically gives the non-primary parent possession on the first, third, and fifth weekends, Thursday evenings, and alternating holidays.

items.q: How can I modify my current custody or visitation order?
items.a: You can request a modification when there has been a material and substantial change in circumstances since the last order — such as a move, a change in a parent's situation, or the child's needs. The change must still serve the child's best interest.

items.q: How is child support calculated in Texas?
items.a: Texas uses statutory guidelines based on the paying parent's net monthly resources and the number of children — generally 20% of net resources for one child, increasing with additional children. Courts can deviate from the guidelines in certain circumstances.

items.q: What do I do if the other parent stops paying child support?
items.a: You can file an enforcement action. Texas courts have powerful tools to compel payment, including wage garnishment, license suspension, interception of tax refunds, and even contempt of court, which can carry jail time.

items.q: Can my child support amount be changed if my income changes?
items.a: Yes. If there has been a material and substantial change — such as a significant income change — or if it has been three years since the last order and the amount would change by a set threshold, you can request a modification.

items.q: How long does child support last in Texas?
items.a: Child support generally continues until the child turns 18 or graduates from high school, whichever is later. Support may continue indefinitely for a child with a disability that requires ongoing care.

items.q: What are my rights if a CPS caseworker comes to my door?
items.a: You have the right to ask for identification, to know the allegations, and to consult an attorney before answering questions or allowing a home visit. In most cases you are not required to let a caseworker into your home without a court order. Contact a lawyer immediately.

items.q: Do I have to sign a CPS Safety Plan?
items.a: A Safety Plan is generally voluntary, but declining can have consequences. These plans can significantly restrict your parental rights. It's important to speak with an attorney before signing anything so you understand exactly what you're agreeing to.

items.q: Can CPS take my children without a court order?
items.a: CPS can remove children without a prior court order only in emergencies where there is an immediate danger to the child's safety. Even then, they must promptly seek court approval. If your children have been removed, you should seek legal representation right away.

items.q: How can I fight false allegations from CPS?
items.a: An experienced attorney can help you respond appropriately, gather evidence, present your side, and protect your rights throughout the investigation and any court proceedings. Do not attempt to navigate a CPS case alone.

items.q: What should I do immediately after a car accident?
items.a: Ensure everyone's safety and call 911. Seek medical attention even if you feel fine, document the scene with photos, exchange information, and get a police report. Avoid admitting fault and contact an attorney before speaking with insurance adjusters.

items.q: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Texas?
items.a: In most cases, Texas has a two-year statute of limitations from the date of the injury. Missing this deadline usually means losing your right to recover compensation, so it's important to act promptly.

items.q: What evidence is most important for my personal injury claim?
items.a: Key evidence includes the police report, medical records, photos of the scene and injuries, witness statements, and documentation of lost wages and expenses. The sooner an attorney gets involved, the more evidence can be preserved.

items.q: Should I talk to the other party's insurance company?
items.a: It's best not to give a recorded statement to the other party's insurer before consulting an attorney. Adjusters are trained to minimize payouts, and early statements can be used to reduce or deny your claim.

items.q: How much is my personal injury case worth?
items.a: Every case is different. Value depends on the severity of injuries, medical costs, lost income, long-term impact, and available insurance. An attorney can evaluate your specific situation after reviewing the facts and medical documentation.

items.q: What types of damages can I recover?
items.a: You may be able to recover economic damages (medical bills, lost wages, property damage) and non-economic damages (pain and suffering, disfigurement, loss of enjoyment of life). In rare cases involving gross negligence, punitive damages may apply.

items.q: How does a personal injury lawyer get paid?
items.a: We handle personal injury cases on a contingency fee basis. That means you pay nothing upfront, and we only get paid if we recover compensation for you — our fee comes as a percentage of the recovery.

items.q: Will my case go to trial, or will it settle?
items.a: Most personal injury cases settle out of court. However, we prepare every case as if it will go to trial. That readiness gives you maximum leverage in settlement negotiations and ensures we're prepared if a fair settlement isn't offered.

items.q: How long does it take to resolve a personal injury case?
items.a: Some cases resolve in a few months, while others — particularly those with serious injuries or disputed liability — can take a year or more. We focus on getting the best result, not just the fastest one.

items.q: What if I were partially at fault for the accident?
items.a: Texas follows a modified comparative fault rule. You can still recover damages as long as you were not more than 50% at fault, though your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault.

items.q: What happens if the at-fault driver doesn't have insurance?
items.a: You may be able to recover through your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage if you have it. We can help identify all available sources of compensation for your injuries.

items.q: Can I sue for a slip and fall accident on someone else's property?
items.a: Possibly. Property owners have a duty to maintain reasonably safe conditions. If they knew or should have known about a hazard and failed to address it, they may be liable for resulting injuries under premises liability law.

items.q: What is a wrongful death claim, and who can file one?
items.a: A wrongful death claim seeks compensation when a person dies due to another's negligence. In Texas, the surviving spouse, children, and parents of the deceased may file such a claim, typically within two years of the death.
